title: The Burden of Choice
paragraphs: Few people in history have had as many options as we have. A shopper in a modern supermarket can choose between dozens of kinds of cereal, a student can pick from thousands of courses online, and a viewer can scroll through a catalogue of films so large that it could not be watched in a lifetime. We tend to assume that more is better, and that a person with ten options is freer than one with three. Experience, however, does not always bear out that assumption.

In 2004, the psychologist Barry Schwartz popularised the idea under the title The Paradox of Choice. His argument was that, beyond a certain point, abundance produces anxiety rather than satisfaction. Faced with too many alternatives, we fear making the wrong decision, we spend more time deciding and we feel less content with our eventual choice, since we cannot stop thinking of what we gave up. The idea resonated widely, and it was often illustrated by an experiment involving jars of jam.

That experiment, conducted in 2000, reported that shoppers were more likely to stop at a display of twenty-four jams but more likely to buy when only six were offered. It is a neat result, and neat results deserve suspicion. Later attempts to reproduce it have had mixed outcomes, and some researchers now think that the effect appears only under particular conditions, such as when options are hard to compare. The paradox may be real, but it is not universal.

What does seem sturdy is the distinction between two kinds of decision-maker. Some people, whom psychologists call maximisers, want the best possible option and search exhaustively; others, called satisficers, are content with one that is good enough. Maximisers often obtain slightly better outcomes, but they tend to be less happy with them. Rarely does the gain compensate for the cost in peace of mind, particularly for decisions of modest importance.

The practical lesson is not that we should want fewer choices, which would be a strange demand in a free society. It is that we should become more deliberate about when to choose carefully. Selecting a university or a house deserves research, comparison and perhaps an anxious night. Selecting a sandwich does not. Anyone who has stood paralysed in front of a menu will recognise the relief of deciding, in advance, that a decision is not worth the energy.

Institutions have a role as well. A well-designed system narrows the field without removing freedom: it offers a sensible default, groups options in meaningful categories or highlights the few that suit most people. Retirement plans, for instance, often work better when they suggest a standard path that individuals may leave, rather than presenting a bare list of dozens of funds. Good design, in this sense, is a form of kindness.

I do not wish to romanticise limits. People who have too few choices, because of poverty or oppression, are in no position to be consoled by the paradox. Yet it is worth remembering that freedom is not measured by the length of the menu. It consists in being able to choose well, and sometimes the wisest use of that freedom is to say, with a shrug and a smile, that the first reasonable option will do.
glossary: persona que se conforma con una opción suficientemente buena

title: Against the Tyranny of Ratings
paragraphs: The other evening, I decided to find a restaurant in Lima, and spent twenty minutes comparing numbers. One place had 4.6 stars from nine hundred reviews; another had 4.7 from sixty. A third had 4.4, but one reviewer called it the best meal of her life. By the end, I was so exhausted by the arithmetic that I ate at home. It was, I admit, a revealing evening.

Star ratings promise something attractive: the wisdom of crowds, reduced to a single digit. In principle, if enough people vote, individual quirks cancel out and the truth emerges. Sometimes it does. A hotel with a thousand reviews averaging 2.1 is almost certainly bad. But the technique works best at the extremes, and most choices happen in the crowded middle, where the difference between 4.4 and 4.6 means almost nothing.

The problem is that ratings measure something other than quality. They measure expectations, mood and, increasingly, strategy. A person who expected a cheap meal and received a good one may give five stars; a person who expected a masterpiece and received a very good one may give three. Reviewers punish a late delivery as severely as bad food. And since the system is public, businesses have learnt to encourage, and sometimes to purchase, favourable reviews.

The effect on behaviour is more worrying. Workers who are rated, drivers, couriers, hosts, live with a permanent anxiety that a single bad evaluation will damage their income. Passengers, aware of this, may give top marks out of kindness, which makes the system even less informative. Everyone ends up inflating, and a four-star rating, which should mean good, comes to mean disastrous.

There is also a cultural effect. When all choices are filtered through numbers, we begin to prefer what is safe and widely liked to what is distinctive. The odd little restaurant, the unusual novel and the strange film are penalised for dividing opinion, while the competent and forgettable are rewarded. Optimising for the average is a sure route to a world in which everything is acceptable and nothing is surprising.

I am not suggesting we abolish reviews. Written comments, especially detailed ones, can be very useful, and a pattern of similar complaints is worth heeding. What I propose is a change of habit: read the three-star reviews rather than the extremes, look for specifics rather than adjectives, and give more weight to the opinion of friends whose taste we know. A single sentence from a person we trust is worth a thousand stars from strangers.

As for my own evening, it ended well. The next day, a colleague recommended a small place near her home, describing the dish she always ordered and the cousin who cooked it. I did not look up its rating, and I still do not know what it is. The meal was excellent. Perhaps the best advice I can give is that some things are better left unquantified, and that appetite, like trust, grows best when it is not constantly being measured.

title: The Ghost Students of the Valley
paragraphs: In a rural district in the highlands of Peru, a primary school registered ninety-four pupils last year. When our reporters visited on a Tuesday in October, they counted thirty-one. The head teacher explained that many children were helping with the harvest. Yet when we compared the school's records with those of three neighbouring villages, we found something stranger: a number of names appeared on the registers of two schools simultaneously.

Schools in many countries receive funding according to the number of pupils enrolled. In principle, this is a reasonable way to allocate resources. In practice, it creates an incentive to inflate the numbers. Our investigation reviewed the enrolment records of forty-two schools in one province over four years. In eleven of them, we found a pattern of enrolment that rose sharply in the months before funding was calculated and fell back soon afterwards.

The practice is rarely crude. Pupils who have moved away remain on the books; children who attend irregularly are counted as full-time; and, in a few cases, names appear to have been invented. A former administrator, who spoke on condition of anonymity, told us that headteachers were quietly encouraged to 'keep the numbers healthy'. 'Nobody thought of it as stealing,' she said. 'It felt like surviving.'

That explanation is not as far-fetched as it sounds. Many of these schools lack basic supplies, and some are staffed by a single teacher covering several grades. A modest increase in funding may mean the difference between buying textbooks and going without. We found no evidence that any of the money was used for personal gain. Nonetheless, the practice distorts the data on which national planning is based, and it diverts resources from schools that report their numbers honestly.

The education authority acknowledged irregularities in its records but said that it had no evidence of systematic fraud. A spokesman said that inspectors visited a sample of schools each year and that any discrepancies were investigated. When we asked how many cases had resulted in action, he said the figure was not immediately available. We have asked again, twice, and are still waiting for the answer.

The consequences are felt most acutely by the pupils who are real. In one village, a teacher showed us a classroom designed for thirty, where forty-three children sat on benches pushed together. The school's official enrolment, he said, was lower, so the funding it received was too small to buy more desks. 'The ghosts do not need chairs,' he said wryly, 'but the children do.'

Experts who study education funding argue that the problem lies in the design of the system rather than in the character of teachers. Funding formulas based solely on headcount invite manipulation. Alternatives exist, including funding based on need, with regular, unannounced attendance checks. These measures are not cheap, but neither is the present arrangement, which pays for pupils who are not there while leaving those who are without desks.

title: A Label Too Easily Worn
paragraphs: When One Hundred Years of Solitude appeared in 1967, readers around the world were captivated by a village in which a priest levitates after drinking hot chocolate and a plague of insomnia erases memory. Critics soon found a phrase to describe such scenes: magical realism. The label stuck, and it has been attached ever since to an enormous variety of Latin American writers, some of whom disliked it and many of whom wrote nothing of the kind.

The term did not originate with García Márquez. The Cuban writer Alejo Carpentier had earlier argued that Latin America's history and landscape were so extraordinary that the marvellous was a part of real life, and he called the idea lo real maravilloso. Juan Rulfo's Pedro Páramo, published in 1955, which is populated by the voices of the dead, had been admired for years. When the novel of 1967 appeared, there was already a tradition waiting for a name.

The label has real value. It points to a way of writing in which the fantastic is narrated with the same calm tone as the everyday, without surprise or explanation. A character may ascend to heaven while folding laundry, and the narrator simply continues. This deadpan quality creates a distinctive effect, and it was a genuine innovation. Readers of Isabel Allende's The House of the Spirits, published in 1982, will recognise it at once.

The difficulty is that a convenient label tends to become a cage. Publishers abroad, eager to repeat a success, began to look for magical realism in every Latin American manuscript, and writers whose work was urban, political, ironic or experimental found themselves told that it was insufficiently magical. In other words, the label that opened the door to the region's literature also began to narrow what the world expected from it.

Some writers have openly resisted. They point out that the region is home to detective novels, science fiction, intimate domestic dramas and difficult avant-garde experiments, none of which fits comfortably under the heading. There is also the awkward suggestion, sometimes implied, that Latin America is a place where the supernatural is part of daily life, an idea that flatters foreign readers' fantasies more than it describes the continent's reality.

None of this means that the term should be discarded. A good label is a useful tool for conversation, and this one has the virtue of describing a technique rather than a nationality. What is needed is a lighter touch: to use it where it fits, to resist applying it where it does not, and to remember that a literary category is a lens, not a map.

The healthiest sign is that new generations of writers refuse to be sorted so easily. Some borrow the technique with irony; others ignore it altogether and write about call centres, migration or the internet. Their readers, increasingly, do not ask whether the work is magical enough. They ask whether it is good. That, after all, is the only question a label was ever meant to help us to answer.

title: Listening for Whales
paragraphs: In the open ocean, sight is a poor sense. Light fades within a couple of hundred metres, and even in clear water a whale may be only a shadow from a boat's deck. Sound, by contrast, travels exceptionally well in water, much faster and farther than in air. It is no surprise that whales, which spend their lives in this environment, depend on it for communication, navigation and the search for food.

Researchers have taken advantage of this fact. Instead of following animals in boats, an expensive and weather-dependent method, they now deploy hydrophones, underwater microphones that record continuously for months. The technique is known as passive acoustic monitoring, because it listens without disturbing anything. A single device can detect calls from many kilometres away and, unlike a human observer, it does not need to sleep or to wait for good weather.

The recordings contain more than simple noise. Different species produce distinct sounds: the low, long moans of blue whales, the clicks of sperm whales hunting at depth, the complex songs of humpbacks. By identifying these sounds, scientists can learn where animals are, when they migrate and in what numbers. Species that are hard to see, such as those that dive deep or live far from shore, may be tracked more easily by their voices than by sight.

Humpback songs are especially fascinating. Males sing long, structured sequences that evolve over time. Studies of populations in the South Pacific have shown that new song patterns can spread from one group to another, travelling across thousands of kilometres within a few years. This is considered one of the clearest examples of cultural transmission in a non-human species: a song is learned, rather than inherited, and passed on from one singer to the next.

The oceans, however, have become noisier. Ships, seismic surveys and construction at sea add a constant background sound that can mask the calls of whales. Whales may respond by calling louder, by shifting the pitch of their calls or by moving away. Because their communication helps them to find mates, keep in touch with calves and locate food, a persistent increase in noise could affect their survival, though the precise consequences are hard to measure.

Acoustic monitoring can also help to reduce the problem. In some busy shipping lanes, hydrophones detect nearby whales and send alerts, allowing vessels to slow down or alter course. Slower ships are quieter, and they are less likely to collide with animals. Such systems are still limited, and they depend on the cooperation of shipping companies, but early results suggest that they can be effective at modest cost.

What the work reveals, above all, is how much of the ocean's life takes place beyond our senses. For most of history, the sea was a silent surface to us, while below it a conversation was going on. Now, with a few cables and a pair of headphones, we can hear part of it, and the first lesson is a humbling one: that the sea was never silent, and that we have been talking over it all along.

title: The Statistician Who Questions Everything
paragraphs: Lucrecia Vidal is the sort of person who, on hearing that crime has fallen by twenty per cent, asks twenty per cent of what. It is a habit that has made her unpopular with press officers and indispensable to editors. At forty-four, Vidal leads the data team of a newspaper in Buenos Aires, where she spends her days checking numbers that other people have already announced. 'A statistic is a sentence,' she likes to say. 'You can ask whether it is true, and also who wrote it.'

She did not set out to become a journalist. Vidal studied statistics at university and worked for years in a government office, calculating inflation indicators. The work was meticulous, but she grew frustrated by what happened to her figures once they left the building. 'I would see a number I had produced quoted in the newspaper, without its caveats, and attached to a conclusion that it did not support,' she recalls. 'It was like seeing your child dressed in somebody else's clothes.'

In her first year at the newspaper, Vidal developed a simple method that her team still follows. Before publishing any figure, the reporter must answer four questions. Where does it come from? What exactly was measured? Compared with what? And what is missing? The last question, she insists, is the most valuable. A study of satisfied customers, for instance, says nothing about those who left, and an average income may conceal enormous differences between the richest and the poorest.

The method has produced some uncomfortable stories. A widely cited figure about public spending on a social programme turned out, on inspection, to include money that had been allocated but never paid. A claim by a company that its product 'reduced complaints by half' was based on a change in how complaints were counted. In each case, Vidal's team published a correction, and in each case, she insists, the aim was not to embarrass anyone but to restore the facts.

She is equally severe with her own side. When her newspaper published a survey claiming that most young people supported a certain policy, Vidal noticed that only 120 people had been interviewed, all of them online. She persuaded the editors to add a note about the sample, over some resistance. 'Nobody likes the note,' she says, 'but it is the part of the article that tells the reader how much to trust the rest.'

Vidal also teaches, giving free workshops to schoolteachers and to local journalists across the country. She tells them that mathematical skill is less important than suspicion, and that suspicion need not be cynical. 'It is not that every number is false,' she says. 'It is that every number has a history, and the history matters.' Her handouts include a page titled 'Ten Tricks with Charts', which has been photocopied so often that it has become, she jokes, her most widely read work.

Asked whether she ever tires of doubting, Vidal laughs and admits that she does. On Sundays she refuses to check any figure, and she goes to watch football with her brother, where, she says, she accepts every statistic that is shouted at her. Then she pauses. 'Well, nearly every one,' she corrects herself, and reaches for her phone to look up how many goals the striker has actually scored this season.

title: Night Shift at the Observatory
focus: Narrative tenses, inversion and participle clauses
paragraphs: The night technician at the observatory was, by contract, the only human being on the mountain between ten in the evening and six in the morning. Inés Carvajal had held the post for three years, and she had learned to like the solitude the way one learns to like a strong coffee. The telescopes, on their pale domes, worked without her; her job was to watch the instruments, to deal with faults and to be, in the event of an emergency, somebody.

The mountain, in northern Chile, rose to a height at which the air was thin and dry, and the sky was so dark that the Milky Way cast faint shadows on the ground. Tourists who visited by day sometimes asked whether she was bored. She never knew how to answer. Boredom, she thought, belonged to places where something was expected to happen, and here nothing was expected, which made the smallest event unusually vivid.

On a night in June, she was making her round of the control room when an alarm sounded. A sensor on the second dome had reported a drop in pressure. She climbed the stairs two at a time, the cold biting her face, and found nothing wrong. The sensor, it turned out, had failed. Yet she stayed for a moment, her breath rising in pale clouds, and looked at the sky through the open slit of the dome. There, a single light was moving.

It was not a plane. Planes blinked, and this did not. It travelled in a steady line from the west, neither hurrying nor slowing, and she realised after a minute that she was looking at a satellite, one of the thousands that now crossed the sky each night. A second followed it, then a third, evenly spaced, like beads on a thread. She watched until the line ended behind the dome.

She had read, of course, about the concern of astronomers. The satellites left bright streaks across long exposures, and they could ruin hours of observation. She had sympathised, in the abstract. Now, standing under them, she felt something that was not quite anger. It was closer to the feeling of finding a stranger's footprints in a garden one had thought was private. The sky, which had seemed to belong to nobody, had acquired traffic.

In the morning, she wrote a short note in the logbook and went to bed at seven, as always. The telescopes, she knew, would work around the problem, with software that removed the streaks and schedules that avoided the busiest hours. The people who ran them were clever and stubborn, and she believed in them. But she thought about the line of lights for a long time before she fell asleep, and she did not find that she minded the thinking.

The following night, she went up to the dome again at the same hour. The satellites came on schedule, a little earlier than the day before. Beyond them, behind them and above them, the stars carried on as they had for billions of years, indifferent and entirely patient. Inés watched both for a while, the new lights and the old ones, and found that there was room in her attention for each.

questions.explain_es: El texto dice: 'The sensor, it turned out, had failed'; no había nada malo.

title: Public Transport Accessibility Audit: Summary
paragraphs: ## 1. Purpose

This summary reports the results of an accessibility audit of the public bus network in a medium-sized Peruvian city. The audit was carried out by a team including two wheelchair users and one person with a visual impairment, who travelled on thirty-five routes over a period of four weeks. Its aim was to assess how far the network allows people with reduced mobility, as well as older people and parents with prams, to travel independently.
## 2. Findings: vehicles

Of the 212 buses inspected, only 38 (18 per cent) were fitted with a functioning ramp. In seven cases, the ramp was present but could not be deployed, usually because it was blocked or damaged. Priority seating was marked in 91 per cent of vehicles, but in nearly half of the journeys observed, these seats were occupied by passengers who did not appear to need them, and drivers did not intervene.

Audible announcements of stops were available on only 12 per cent of buses. For passengers with visual impairments, this constitutes a significant barrier, as they depend on the driver or other passengers to indicate their stop. Auditors reported that drivers were generally courteous, but that their responses varied considerably from one route to another.
## 3. Findings: infrastructure

Of the 150 bus stops assessed, 64 per cent had no shelter, and 41 per cent lacked a seat. Kerbs were higher than ten centimetres at more than half of the stops, making boarding from a wheelchair impossible without help. Pavements leading to stops were frequently obstructed by parked vehicles, street vendors or damaged paving. In the three districts furthest from the centre, none of the stops was fully accessible.

Interviews with 60 regular users with disabilities complemented the physical inspection. Half of them said that they avoided public transport altogether, relying instead on relatives or on taxis that cost them, on average, a quarter of their monthly income. Those who did use buses reported that they planned each journey in advance, checking which routes had ramps and travelling only at off-peak times, a level of preparation that other passengers are rarely asked to make.
## 4. Cost and recommendations

The authors estimate that bringing the network to a basic standard of accessibility would cost approximately 18 million soles over five years, equivalent to roughly 4 per cent of the current annual transport budget. They recommend that the city adopt a phased plan, beginning with the ten routes carrying the largest number of passengers, and that all new vehicles purchased be fitted with ramps and audible announcements.

The audit also recommends that drivers receive training in assisting passengers with disabilities, and that a simple complaints system be established, so that users can report problems without having to visit an office. Finally, the authors stress that accessibility measures benefit a wide range of passengers, including parents with prams and older travellers, and should therefore not be regarded as a specialised service for a small group.

questions.q: What can be inferred from the fact that priority seats were often occupied by other passengers?
options: Drivers were always strict about the rule
Marking seats is not enough without enforcement
Passengers with disabilities do not use buses
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: los asientos estaban señalizados en el 91 por ciento de los buses, pero los conductores no intervenían; la señal sola no basta.

questions.q: How does the report describe the drivers?
questions.explain_es: Tono/actitud: eran 'generally courteous' pero 'their responses varied considerably from one route to another'.

questions.q: Why does the report mention that measures benefit many passengers?
options: To argue that accessibility is of general value
questions.explain_es: Propósito: subraya que la accesibilidad beneficia a padres con cochecitos y personas mayores, y no es un servicio especializado.

By the dates of the inspections

title: On Apologising Well
paragraphs: There is a kind of apology that makes things worse. We have all heard it: 'I am sorry if anyone was offended.' It sounds like an apology, but it is built to avoid one. The 'if' casts doubt on whether harm was done, the passive 'was offended' removes the person responsible, and the vague 'anyone' suggests that the injured party is a small and oversensitive minority. Seldom has a sentence contained so much in so few words.

Why do we do this? Partly because a real apology is exposed. To say clearly what one did, and that it was wrong, is to accept that one might be judged, and perhaps punished. Defensiveness is a reflex, as natural as raising a hand against a blow. Yet the cost of the reflex is high, since a grudging apology often angers the other person more than silence would have done.

What, then, makes an apology good? Philosophers and psychologists have offered several lists, but the elements most often named are remarkably consistent. First, an honest account of what happened, without euphemism. Second, an acknowledgement of the harm caused, in the other person's terms rather than one's own. Third, an expression of regret that does not shift attention to the apologiser's feelings. Finally, some indication of what will change, whether by repairing the damage or by avoiding repetition.

What is conspicuously absent from this list is the word 'but'. 'I am sorry, but you must understand the pressure I was under' is not an apology; it is a defence with a polite introduction. Explanations have their place, and sometimes the other person needs one. But an explanation offered before the apology reads as an excuse, while one offered afterwards, and only on request, may help to restore trust.

Institutions face the same challenge on a larger scale. A company that has sold a faulty product or a government that has made a grave error is tempted to issue statements full of passive verbs and carefully tested language. Audiences have become adept at recognising the form. Nothing damages credibility faster than a sentence in which mistakes were made by nobody in particular, and corrective measures will be looked into at some future date.

It is worth saying, too, that apology is not always owed, and that demanding one can be a form of pressure. Some conflicts involve genuine disagreement rather than wrongdoing, and an insincere apology, extracted to keep the peace, is a poor foundation for anything. A good apology must be freely given. For that reason, the most useful habit is not the readiness to say sorry but the willingness to ask honestly whether one has anything to be sorry for.

If apologising well is difficult, it is also rewarding. People who can say clearly, 'I did this, it hurt you, and I will do better,' tend to be trusted more afterwards, not less. The paradox is only apparent: an admission of fault is evidence of a character that can be relied upon to notice its own faults. It is a small act of courage, and it is almost always worth the discomfort.

questions.explain_es: Afirma que con 'but' no es una disculpa sino 'a defence with a polite introduction'.

questions.q: The author believes an apology should be freely given and not forced.
questions.explain_es: Dice que 'A good apology must be freely given' y que una disculpa forzada es 'a poor foundation'.

questions.q: What does the author imply about the sentence 'I am sorry if anyone was offended'?
options: It is the clearest form of apology
questions.explain_es: Inferencia: la frase 'is built to avoid' una disculpa: duda del daño, omite a la persona responsable y minimiza al afectado.

questions.q: How would you describe the author's tone?
options: Analytical, with a touch of wit
questions.explain_es: Tono: analiza con ejemplos y un toque de humor ('mistakes were made by nobody in particular').

questions.q: Why does the author discuss companies and governments?
options: To argue that institutions never apologise
To show the same problem on a larger scale
questions.explain_es: Propósito: muestra que el problema de las disculpas evasivas se repite 'on a larger scale' en las instituciones.

questions.q: How does the final paragraph resolve the essay?
options: By suggesting that an honest apology builds trust
questions.explain_es: Estructura: concluye que una disculpa honesta tiende a generar más confianza, y que la paradoja 'is only apparent'.

questions.q: In 'a remarkably consistent list', 'consistent' means…
questions.explain_es: 'Consistent' es coherente: los elementos se repiten de forma similar en distintas listas.
